issues.subcategory: Abstract timeframe is narrower than the reported delays
issues.description: Abstract timeframe is narrower than the reported delays: “Within this timeframe” points readers to a 1–2 s interval, but the main delay contrasts are 0.75 s versus 3 s in Experiment 1 and 0.5 s versus 3 s in later experiments. The claim would be safer if the abstract said “within a few seconds” or “over delays from about 0.5–0.75 s to 3 s”. That matches the methods without changing the substantive message.
issues.quote: However, it is generally assumed that short-term memory for percepts formed just 1 or 2 seconds ago accurately represents the percepts as they were at the time of perception. Here 4 experiments consistently show that within this timeframe, participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there (memory report strongly influenced by top-down expectations).

issues.subcategory: Overstatement of initial reporting accuracy
issues.description: Overstatement of initial reporting accuracy: The Abstract’s “go from reliably reporting what was there ... to erroneously ... reporting what they expected to be there” somewhat overstates the accuracy of the earliest probes. In the results, high-confidence pseudo-to-real errors are already substantial at the shortest delays, for example about 29% for pseudo-letter targets at 0.75 s in Experiment 1 and 25% at 0.5 s in Experiment 2. The evidence supports an increase in such errors over the retention interval, but not a clean transition from initially accurate reporting to later illusory reporting.
issues.quote: Here 4 experiments consistently show that within this timeframe, participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there (memory report strongly influenced by top-down expectations).

issues.subcategory: Scope of STM claim in the Introduction
issues.description: Scope of STM claim in the Introduction: The phrase “STM in general” appears broader than the evidence can establish. The paragraph defines STM as covering iconic memory, fragile memory, working memory, and durations from sub-500 ms to minutes, whereas the experiments test visual letter memory over short retention intervals. This creates some risk of overstating the scope of the empirical claim, especially given the later acknowledgement that iconic memory is not tested.
issues.quote: STM is an umbrella term for memory that stores information for a short period of time (seconds to minutes). Different types of STM have different capacity and time-limits. STM is often hypothesized to consist of short-lived ( $<500 \mathrm{~ms}$ ) iconic memory and longer lasting working memory. Sligte and colleagues have additionally suggested the presence of an intermediate form of STM, namely fragile memory, which, like WM, lasts at least 4 seconds, but unlike WM has a capacity of $5-15$ items. Here, we present 4 studies that explore whether STM in general is susceptible to false memories just like LTM has been shown to be.

issues.subcategory: Overgeneralisation about STM error interpretation
issues.description: Overgeneralisation about STM error interpretation: The claim that failures to report recently presented information are “seldom interpreted as a memory error” is too broad. It is defensible for some perception or psychophysics contexts where STM reports are used as a proxy for perception, but visual working memory research routinely treats brief-delay report failures as memory limitations, decay, interference, noise, or binding errors.
issues.quote: This illustrates the general assumption that STM is a highly reliable storage of recent events: failures to correctly report information that was only recently presented is seldom interpreted as a memory error, but usually seen as a perceptual error.

issues.subcategory: LTM evidence paragraph slightly overclaims “world knowledge alone”
issues.description: LTM evidence paragraph slightly overclaims “world knowledge alone”: The phrase “world knowledge alone” appears too strong in this paragraph. As described, the Kleider and gender-occupation examples involve experimentally supplied roles or occupations, so they more directly show that internal expectations bias memory for contextual information than that prior knowledge alone generates the relevant false content.
issues.quote: Indeed, some studies show that world knowledge alone (such as knowledge about social roles) is sufficient to generate memory errors. For example, Kleider and colleagues showed participants faces combined with roles (professor, drug dealer, artist). After a 20 -minute delay, participants were more likely to incorrectly attribute criminal labels to faces with stereotypically black features. This suggests that an internal bias associating black faces with crime can shape memory. Similar effects were shown for male and female names that were linked to gender-(in)consistent occupations : illusory recollections were more likely to follow gender-based expectations. These results suggest that both external, contextual information and internal expectations about the world can change the content of LTM, resulting in illusory memories.

issues.subcategory: High confidence is treated as too diagnostic
issues.description: High confidence is treated as too diagnostic: High-confidence errors are a useful operational filter for excluding low-confidence guesses, but the passage appears to treat confidence as more diagnostic of an actual false memory trace than it can be on its own. A high-confidence error could also reflect a confident inference, familiarity-based choice, or metacognitive miscalibration when the trace is degraded, so confidence alone does not fully distinguish trace alteration from other high-certainty post-perceptual processes.
issues.quote:
Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace). In the absence of confidence ratings, the erroneous responses could actually consist of low confidence responses or even outright guesses. In these cases, the response is most likely not the result of an illusory memory. Instead, it is more likely to result from the absence of a reliable memory, which is compensated
by conscious inferences about what is likely to have occurred. Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: Conflating high confidence with episodic recollection
issues.description: Conflating high confidence with episodic recollection: The passage risks conflating high confidence with the phenomenology of remembering a perceptual episode. High confidence can exclude many low-confidence guesses, but it can also arise from strong semantic or familiarity-based ‘knowing’ about what is likely, especially for overlearned letters. Without a measure that separates recollective experience from confident knowing or inference, high-confidence errors should not be treated as definitively isolating perceptual false memories.
issues.quote:
In the absence of confidence ratings, the erroneous responses could actually consist of low confidence responses or even outright guesses. In these cases, the response is most likely not the result of an illusory memory. Instead, it is more likely to result from the absence of a reliable memory, which is compensated
by conscious inferences about what is likely to have occurred. Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: Over-localisation of delay effects in the design rationale
issues.description: Over-localisation of delay effects in the design rationale: The delay manipulation supports the conclusion that the errors are not fixed solely at initial perception or encoding, but the localisation to processes occurring ‘during STM storage itself’ seems stronger than the design alone establishes. A delay-dependent increase could also arise from retrieval- or decision-stage use of priors when a degraded memory trace is mapped onto the response alternatives, so the evidence more directly supports a post-perceptual, memory-dependent account than a specifically storage-stage mechanism.
issues.quote: To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM - since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed. Therefore, if the number of reported illusions increases as the retention interval increases, this is best explained by memory-related processes taking place during the retention interval, so during STM storage itself, and not in the perceptual or encoding process. Moreover, we exclude the possibility that the errors are a result of guessing in the absence of reliable memories / reliable perception by focusing on high confidence errors: errors where the participant explicitly indicates to know the answer, and has not just guessed.

issues.subcategory: Hypotheses paragraph blurs report timing
issues.description: Hypotheses paragraph blurs report timing: The hypotheses paragraph appears to conflate the time of cue/probe onset with the time of the overt identity response and confidence judgement. In several conditions, participants report only after a later irrelevant display, even though the target is cued earlier. Because the timing claim is central to the perception-versus-memory distinction, the paper should distinguish more explicitly between when the memory is probed and when the high-confidence report is made.
issues.quote: In 4 experiments we thus test 3 hypotheses: 1) Illusions occur in STM: high confidence reports of having seen a real letter when a pseudo-letter was shown, or vice versa, occur within $1-2$ seconds after a memory display has disappeared. 2) These reports reflect illusory memories, and are not the result of incorrect perceptual encoding: the high confidence illusory reports become more prevalent as memory deteriorates, through the passage of time or through interference , and 3) The illusory memories are driven by world knowledge: high confidence illusory reports are more likely to involve pseudo-letter to real-letter errors (as real letters are well-studied and much more prevalent in the real world) than the other way around.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory description of training trial sequence
issues.description: Contradictory description of training trial sequence: The training-task timing does not fully specify the memory-test SOA for each cue condition. The text first suggests a serial blank–cue–test sequence, but then says the cue sometimes appeared with the test display and sometimes during the blank interval, leaving the onset of the test display relative to cue onset and offset unclear.
issues.quote: This was followed by a blank screen of $0.1-1$ seconds, a cue for 0.5 seconds and a test display, which remained visible until response. The memory and test display were identical, except that the orientation of the rectangle at the cued location differed 90 degrees between both displays on a randomly selected $50 \%$ of the trials. The cue appeared either 100 milliseconds, or 1 second after offset of the memory display. In some trials the cue appeared during a blank interval in between memory display and test display, in other trials the cue appeared together with the test display.

issues.subcategory: Missing trial counts for training blocks
issues.description: Missing trial counts for training blocks: The training exclusion rule is under-specified: the criterion is calculated over the final 10 blocks, but the number of trials per block and the total amount of training administered are not given. Because the denominator affects the strictness of the >75% threshold and reproducibility of the screening procedure, these details should be reported.
issues.quote: Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than $75 \%$ correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training.

issues.subcategory: Critical-trial logic in Experiment 1 Stimuli
issues.description: Critical-trial logic in Experiment 1 Stimuli: The Experiment 1 description of critical trials is potentially ambiguous. The probability statements indicate that critical trials were target-absent response displays in which the mirrored counterpart replaced the correct target, making “none of these” the correct response; however, “combined with its mirrored counterpart” could be read as if both target and counterpart appeared. Because this distinction changes what an illusory error measures, the operational definition should be pinned down.
issues.quote:
The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

The target letter was a real letter in $75 \%$ of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining $25 \%$. If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected $83 \%$ of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other $16 \%$ of the trials. This ensured that of the critical trials (trials where participants could exhibit memory illusion: trials in which a real- or pseudo-letter target was combined with its mirrored counterpart in the response screen) about half were real-to-pseudo trials (approximately $13 \%$ of all trials), while the other half were pseudo-to-real trials (again, approximately $13 \%$ of all trials).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 response screens and critical trials are described inconsistently
issues.description: Experiment 1 response screens and critical trials are described inconsistently: The first sentence reads as if every response display contained the target, either in its original orientation or mirrored. The next paragraph instead says that on some trials the target itself was absent and only the mirrored counterpart was available. This distinction matters: selecting the counterpart when the true target is absent is a different decision from choosing the counterpart over an available correct target, and this changes what an illusory error measures. Please spell out the response-screen construction separately for target-present and counterpart-only trials, and revise the definition of “critical trials” so it is clear whether the target and counterpart were both shown or whether the counterpart replaced the target.

The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 critical-trial percentages do not follow from the stated probabilities
issues.description: Experiment 1 critical-trial percentages do not follow from the stated probabilities: Using the stated probabilities, pseudo-to-real critical trials are 0.25 × 0.50 = 12.5% of all trials, and real-to-pseudo critical trials are 0.75 × 0.16 = 12%. That totals 24.5%, or 25% if 16% is a rounded one-sixth. The reported 26% and “~220 trials” should be replaced with exact counts and percentages from the implemented design, especially because these trials define the main error measures.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in $75 \%$ of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining $25 \%$. If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected $83 \%$ of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other $16 \%$ of the trials. This ensured that of the critical trials (trials where participants could exhibit memory illusion: trials in which a real- or pseudo-letter target was combined with its mirrored counterpart in the response screen) about half were real-to-pseudo trials (approximately $13 \%$ of all trials), while the other half were pseudo-to-real trials (again, approximately $13 \%$ of all trials). Together, the critical trials made up $\sim 220$ trials, $26 \%$ of all trials in the experiment.

issues.subcategory: Probe-to-second-display interval mixes onset and offset timing
issues.description: Probe-to-second-display interval mixes onset and offset timing: The stated 1.5 s and 3.75 s intervals are correct only if the interval is measured from probe offset to second-display onset. Onset-to-onset intervals would be 2 s in the Long condition and 4.25 s in the Short condition. Please specify “blank interval from probe offset to second-display onset” so that the timing can be replicated without guesswork.
issues.quote: If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset, which meant that the interval between the probe and the irrelevant second display was either presented for 1.5 s (Long delay) or 3.75 s (short delay). In all cases, the memory probe was shown for 0.5 seconds and the irrelevant second display was presented for 0.5 seconds.

issues.subcategory: Set size is collapsed without explanation in Analysis
issues.description: Set size is collapsed without explanation in Analysis: Experiment 1 appears to collapse across set size without reporting whether it was tested or why it was treated as a nuisance factor. Because 6- and 8-item displays differ in memory load and in pseudo-letter composition, an unreported set-size effect or interaction could affect the interpretation of the delay and target-type effects, even if the main conclusions are later supported by other experiments.
issues.quote:
Analysis
For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants ( 17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions. Included participants had on average $53.8 \%$ high confidence trials over all critical conditions (range: $36.3-93.2$, sd: 13.9). Excluded participants had on average $26.2 \%$ high confidence trials over all conditions (range $3.6-47.7 \%$, sd: 13.0 ).

issues.subcategory: Uncorrected baseline for "other errors" vs "illusory errors"
issues.description: Uncorrected baseline for "other errors" vs "illusory errors": There seems to be an issue with the baseline for “other errors”: if this measure aggregates selections across several non-counterpart response options, it should not be interpreted as directly comparable to selection of the single mirrored counterpart at the per-option level. This does not undermine the conservative pseudo-to-real comparison, but it would affect claims that equal aggregate rates for real-letter targets mean no special tendency to choose the counterpart.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: Imprecise Bayesian model-comparison wording in Analysis
issues.description: Imprecise Bayesian model-comparison wording in Analysis: The Bayesian ANOVA description uses non-standard model-comparison wording. In JASP, BFm reflects the change from prior to posterior model odds for a model, rather than a comparison with a model’s “prior explanatory value”; likewise, “best fit” may obscure that Bayesian model evidence balances fit against complexity. Because later results rely on BFm and BFincl, this description should be made more statistically precise.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type. Within this analysis, the posterior odds of all different combinations the three factors and their interactions are compared to the prior explanatory value of each model. Based on this analysis, we selected the model with the best fit, reporting the BFm. Individual model components (main effects and interactions) were additionally evaluated based on their BFincl across all models.

issues.subcategory: Hypothesis 3 is not tested by the stated contrast
issues.description: Hypothesis 3 is not tested by the stated contrast: The stated question is whether pseudo-to-real errors occur more often than real-to-pseudo errors. A Target Type × Error Type interaction is a difference-in-differences: it asks whether the gap between mirror-counterpart errors and other errors differs by target type. That is related, but it is not the direct pseudo-to-real versus real-to-pseudo contrast. For instance, the interaction could change because unrelated “other” errors differ by target type. Report the direct contrast of mirror-counterpart error rates for pseudo-letter versus real-letter targets, or rephrase the hypothesis test as a difference-in-differences against other errors.
issues.quote: We investigated our three main hypotheses: hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? - by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors (main effect of Error Type). We tested our second hypothesis - do illusions increase as memory deteriorates? - by measuring if illusions increased from the Short to the other memory conditions (interaction between Memory Delay and Error Type). Finally, we tested our third hypothesis - does world knowledge drive STM illusions? - by investigating if high confidence errors confusing pseudo-letter targets for their real counterparts occurred more often than the other way around (Target Type interacts with Error Type).

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between hypothesis and statistical test
issues.description: Mismatch between hypothesis and statistical test: The mapping of Hypothesis 2 to the Memory Delay $\times$ Error Type interaction is slightly imprecise. That interaction tests whether illusory errors increase differently, or more, than other high-confidence errors across delay/interference conditions; it does not by itself test only whether illusory errors increase in absolute terms.
issues.quote: We tested our second hypothesis - do illusions increase as memory deteriorates? - by measuring if illusions increased from the Short to the other memory conditions (interaction between Memory Delay and Error Type).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 delay and interference effects are pooled in the interpretation
issues.description: Experiment 1 delay and interference effects are pooled in the interpretation: The reported comparison is Short versus an average of Short-with-interference and Long. That supports a weaker statement than “a larger memory delay or more visual interference” as separate effects. The interaction shows that error type varies across the three conditions, but the text should either give the planned pairwise contrasts for Short versus Long and Short versus Short-with-interference, or describe the pooled comparison more cautiously.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 was supported: Illusions (pseudo-to-real or real-to-pseudo) were much more prevalent than other errors (a main effect of Error Type, BFincl>1000). The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2 : as memory deteriorates with a larger memory delay or more visual interference, the increase in illusory errors ( $7 \%$ increase from 19\% in the short delay to 26\% averaged over the short with interference and long delay) is larger than other errors ( $4 \%$ increase, from 8 to $12 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Anecdotal three-way evidence is described too strongly
issues.description: Anecdotal three-way evidence is described too strongly: The first sentence correctly calls the three-way evidence anecdotal under the paper’s own scale. The next sentence then treats the pseudo-letter illusion increase as a supported differential sensitivity. Keep the cell changes, but mark them as descriptive unless the paper reports stronger evidence for the three-way pattern. This matters because the stronger claim is doing theoretical work later in the paper.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl $=2.45$ ): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase $12 \%$ as memory deteriorates through interference of time or visual information (29\% illusions to 41\% illusions). None of the other conditions are as sensitive for memory decay, with other errors for pseudo-letter targets increasing $3 \%$, and illusory errors and other errors for real letter targets increasing $2 \%$ and $7 \%$, respectively.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 discussion: unclear 70% denominator
issues.description: Experiment 1 discussion: unclear 70% denominator: The $70\%$ correct figure in the Experiment 1 discussion is hard to map onto the reported pseudo-to-real illusion rates and the Experiment 1 response-option structure. Because the actual pseudo-target and its mirrored counterpart were not always available in the same response context, it is unclear whether $70\%$ is calculated over all high-confidence Short pseudo-letter trials, target-present trials, critical trials, or another subset; this matters for the claim that early perception/encoding was relatively intact.
issues.quote: What causes these illusory reports? One option is incorrect perception or encoding when the memory is formed. However, Experiment 1 shows that expectation-induced memory illusions increase as memory declines. From the Short (memory probe 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display with no visual interference) to the Long condition (memory probe after 3 seconds) or the Short with interference (memory probe after .75 seconds following an interfering display) the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from $29 \%$ to $39 \%$ and $43 \%$, respectively. This indicates that high confidence errors are not purely the result of errors in perception or encoding: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in $70 \%$ of high confidence trials, thus showing that initial perceptual encoding was relatively intact.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1: delay evidence may be overinterpreted
issues.description: Experiment 1: delay evidence may be overinterpreted: The delay-related increase in high-confidence illusion rates supports a memory-related interpretation, but the causal wording here seems too strong. Because the reported rates appear to be conditional on high-confidence responses, the increase could partly reflect changes in the composition of high-confidence trials over delay or interference, rather than directly showing that correctly encoded traces are converted into illusory memories during STM storage.
issues.quote: What causes these illusory reports? One option is incorrect perception or encoding when the memory is formed. However, Experiment 1 shows that expectation-induced memory illusions increase as memory declines. From the Short (memory probe 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display with no visual interference) to the Long condition (memory probe after 3 seconds) or the Short with interference (memory probe after .75 seconds following an interfering display) the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from $29 \%$ to $39 \%$ and $43 \%$, respectively. This indicates that high confidence errors are not purely the result of errors in perception or encoding: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in $70 \%$ of high confidence trials, thus showing that initial perceptual encoding was relatively intact. When the memory trace deteriorates, high confidence reports are moving towards an equal division between accurate and illusory memories. This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 response-bias argument needs support
issues.description: Experiment 1 response-bias argument needs support: The response-bias rebuttal relies on low-confidence percentages that are not part of the reported Experiment 1 analysis plan and are given without denominators or inferential evidence. Since the pseudo-to-real versus real-to-pseudo asymmetry is still numerically present at low confidence ($22\%$ vs $17\%$), the passage should be more cautious in treating this descriptive comparison as ruling out response bias unless its reliability and conditioning set are established.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. If the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias (more expectation-induced illusions [ J to C ] than similarity-induced illusions [ C to J]) should be present not only for the high-confidence responses; indeed, it should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses. This is because a response bias is present whether the participant thinks they remembered correctly or not, and a participant ought to rely more heavily on a response bias when they have only a weak memory of what they saw. However, in Experiment 1 the tendency to report more expectation-induced illusions than similarity induced illusions is clearly present in high confidence trials, but is much less pronounced in low confidence trials - an opposite finding to what one would expect if these effects were the result of a response bias: On high confidence trials pseudo-letter targets were more often confused for their real counterparts ( $36 \%$ ) than on low confidence trials ( $22 \%$ ). However, the reverse was observed when real letter targets were confused for their pseudo counterpart (high confidence: $11 \%$, low confidence: $17 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1: response-bias rebuttal is too strong
issues.description: Experiment 1: response-bias rebuttal is too strong: The low-confidence comparison rules out only a simple guessing-based response bias. A familiarity or response-tendency mechanism favouring real letters could also affect subjective confidence, so its signature need not be strongest among responses labelled low confidence. The passage therefore seems too strong in treating the high- versus low-confidence pattern as evidence against response bias in general.
issues.quote: Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters, since real letters are a well-known category. If the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias (more expectation-induced illusions [ J to C ] than similarity-induced illusions [ C to J]) should be present not only for the high-confidence responses; indeed, it should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses. However, the reverse was observed when real letter targets were confused for their pseudo counterpart (high confidence: $11 \%$, low confidence: $17 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Confidence comparison overgeneralises across error directions
issues.description: Confidence comparison overgeneralises across error directions: The final sentence treats the present “memory illusions” as a single class, but the preceding percentages show different confidence patterns for the two directions. Pseudo-to-real errors are higher in high-confidence trials, while real-to-pseudo errors are higher in low-confidence trials. Narrow the comparison to the expectation-congruent pseudo-to-real reports, or explicitly state that the confidence pattern differs by error direction.
issues.quote:
However, in Experiment 1 the tendency to report more expectation-induced illusions than similarity induced illusions is clearly present in high confidence trials, but is much less pronounced in low confidence trials - an opposite finding to what one would expect if these effects were the result of a response bias: On high confidence trials pseudo-letter targets were more often confused for their real counterparts ( $36 \%$ ) than on low confidence trials ( $22 \%$ ). However, the reverse was observed when real letter targets were confused for their pseudo counterpart (high confidence: $11 \%$, low confidence: $17 \%$ ).

This also shows that the current illusory memories are quite different from earlier reports of swap errors in STM , where participants incorrectly report having seen features of a distractor, instead of the target feature. While the currently observed memory illusions are more likely to occur in high confidence trials than on low confidence trials, swap errors generally occur on low confidence trials instead of high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: Transient-expectation prediction is one-sided
issues.description: Transient-expectation prediction is one-sided: If the colour cue creates a transient prior over target category, the natural reciprocal prediction is that a pseudo-letter cue should increase real-to-pseudo errors. If the authors do not expect that, then the manipulation is not a symmetric test of transient expectations; it is a test of whether the colour cue modulates the existing real-letter prior. State which hypothesis is being tested and align the reported analysis with that prediction.
issues.quote: The illusory memories observed in Experiment 1 seem to be driven by world knowledge, i.e. long-standing knowledge about the usual orientation of letters. In Experiment 2, we tested whether transiently induced expectations can also cause illusory memories in STM. To this end, we associated the color of the fixation cross with either a high or a low probability of a pseudo-letter target. If transiently induced expectations can induce illusory memories, then pseudo-to-real illusions should be more prevalent when the fixation color induced the expectation of a real letter target, than when it induces the expectation of a pseudo-letter target.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 “other errors” category needs definition
issues.description: Experiment 2 “other errors” category needs definition: In Experiment 2, the ‘other errors’ level of Error Type is not fully operationalised for the revised six-option response display. Because the non-target alternatives include an uncued memory item, that item’s counterpart, and a novel pair, the Error Type contrast is ambiguous unless it is clear whether all non-target, non-counterpart selections are pooled and whether the reported rate is a pooled class rate rather than a per-option-normalised rate.
issues.quote:
The response screen consisted of 6 letters, 3 real letters and their pseudo counterparts. 2 pairs of letter/pseudo-letters had been part of the memory display (either as real or as pseudo-letter) and 1 pair had not been part of the memory display. The letter at the cued location was always presented in the response display, additionally one of the other letters presented in the memory display was also one of the response options. Since the target letter (and its counterpart) were always among the response options, the response option "none of these" was eliminated. Furthermore, both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: $0.148,0.078$, luminance: $6.47 \mathrm{~cd} / \mathrm{m} 2$ ) or red (CIE: $0.641,0.341$; luminance: 11.9 $\mathrm{cd} / \mathrm{m} 2)$.

## Procedure

Before the actual experiment each participant received instructions about the goal of the task, namely to correctly report the cued letter from the first display. The participant was extensively instructed to not confuse real and pseudo-letters. Furthermore, participants performed 12 practice trials. The practice trials were identical to the experimental trials, except
that the memory display was shown for 2.5 seconds instead of 250 ms . After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance. The main experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 20 trials. After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy. This extensive feedback was provided to keep the participants motivated. See Figure 3 for an overview of the procedure.

Each trial started with the presentation of a fixation cross on an otherwise blank screen for 0.5 seconds. After this, the memory display was presented for 0.25 seconds, a blank screen, only containing the fixation cross was presented for 0.5 (the Short condition) or 3 seconds (the Long condition). Then the cue was presented for 0.25 seconds, again followed by a fixation cross on a blank background. 3.75 seconds after the offset of the memory display, the second display was presented for 0.25 seconds (participants were instructed to ignore this second display). After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1-4). The color of the fixation cross was the same throughout the entire trial, but varied across trials. The color of the fixation cross and the memory cue were identical. If the fixation cross and the cue were red, a pseudo-letter was the target on $25 \%$ of the trials. The target was a pseudo-letter on $60 \%$ of the trials when the fixation cross and the cue were blue. Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses. This experiment contained two memory delay conditions (short and long), two target types (real and pseudo) and two fixation color conditions (red and blue). All conditions were randomly intermixed throughout the experiment.

Analysis
First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors, analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors. Since this analysis showed no effects of cue colour (see Results), the rest of the analysis was conducted while collapsing over the two cue colour conditions. As in Experiment 1, error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type (illusions -from pseudo-to-real or the other way around- vs other errors) as independent variables and relative occurrence of high confidence selection as the dependent variable.

The sentence begins by saying that error rates on high-confidence trials were analysed, but then names the dependent variable as the ‘relative occurrence of high confidence selection’, which could be read as the frequency of high-confidence responding rather than the relative rate of illusory versus other high-confidence errors.

issues.subcategory: Imprecise mapping of Hypothesis 1 to the main effect

Because the ‘illusion’ level includes both pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo counterpart errors, this main effect supports the prevalence of counterpart or illusory errors in general; the specifically directional, expectation-based pseudo-to-real bias is tested by the Target Type × Error Type interaction.
issues.quote: Hypothesis 1 (Illusory memories occur in STM) would be supported if expectation-induced errors are more prevalent than other errors, resulting in a main effect of Error Type.

issues.subcategory: Rate changes are percentage-point changes

From 25% to 33% is an 8 percentage-point change; as a relative increase it is 32%. Use “percentage points” in these comparisons throughout the Results to avoid overstating or mislabelling the size of the effect.
issues.quote: With pseudo-letter targets, a longer memory delay (from Short to Long) generated an $8 \%$ increase of expectation-induced memory illusions (from $25 \%$ to $33 \%$ ). With real letter targets expectation-induced illusions barely increased from short to long delays ( $2 \%$ increase, from $7 \%$ to $9 \%$ ).

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 overstates the world-knowledge conclusion before the balancing control
issues.description: Experiment 2 overstates the world-knowledge conclusion before the balancing control: Experiment 2 controls response-option availability by presenting the target and its counterpart together. It does not yet remove the experiment-long stimulus-frequency concern that motivates Experiment 3. The conclusion should therefore be toned down here. A fairer wording would say that Experiment 2 is consistent with a prior-knowledge account beyond simple response-option availability, and that Experiment 3 tests whether the asymmetry survives when real and pseudo-letter frequencies are balanced.
issues.quote: The results of Experiment 2 moreover clearly indicate that the observed memory illusions are based on world knowledge, and not just on visual similarities between the target and the chosen mirrored counterpart. As in Experiment 1, illusions evoked by a pseudo-letter are more prevalent than illusions induced by a real letter, even when both the pseudo-letter and the real letter are simultaneously present in the response display.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 balancing is underspecified in Methods
issues.description: Experiment 3 balancing is underspecified in Methods: Experiment 3’s target-type balancing is stated in the rationale and Discussion, but the Methods leave its implementation somewhat unclear. Because Experiment 2 included colour-contingent target probabilities, the statement that the procedure was identical to Experiment 2 with only two exceptions makes it uncertain whether that cue/probability manipulation was removed or how the 50/50 real- versus pseudo-letter target balance was enforced.
issues.quote:
To test this, Experiment 3 uses a completely balanced stimulus set: pseudo-letters make up half of each memory display, and are cued as targets in half of the trials.

Experiment 1 and 2 consistently show that participants are more inclined to mistakenly report having seen the real counterpart of a pseudo-letter target, and that these pseudo-to-real illusions are more likely than reporting real-to-pseudo illusions. If this is caused by the unbalanced stimulus sets, then Experiment 3 should show that participants exposed to a balanced stimulus set are equally likely to confuse a pseudo-letter with its real counterpart as the other way around. If, however, the higher incidence of pseudo-to-real letter illusions results from world knowledge that real letters are more common than pseudo-letters, then this difference should be present also when the stimulus set itself is completely balanced with regards to the presence of pseudo- and real letter(-target)s.

## Methods

## Participants

In this experiment, 64 participants participated ( 51 women; age range $17-46$ years, average age 20.5 years), all having normal or corrected-to-normal vision. All participants were naïve to the purpose of this experiment. All participants gave their written informed consent to participate in the study, which was approved by the local ethics review board of the University of Amsterdam. The participants participated for student credits within the first-year Psychology curriculum. Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

Stimuli
The memory displays and irrelevant intervening screens were the same as in Experiment 2 except that the memory displays always consisted of 3 real and 3 pseudo-letters.

## Procedure

The experiment consisted of 18 blocks of 25 trials. The procedure was identical to Experiment 2, with two exceptions.

issues.subcategory: Sequential Bayes-factor stopping rule is under-specified
issues.description: Sequential Bayes-factor stopping rule is under-specified: The stopping rule is part of the method because it determined the sample size. The description should state whether the monitored quantity was BF10 or BF01, what prior and t-test settings were used, whether there was a stopping boundary for evidence favouring the null, and whether any minimum or maximum sample size was set. “Crossed a BF of 10” is not enough for another group to reproduce the sampling rule.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets. Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 3 final ANOVA sample size is unclear
issues.description: Experiment 3 final ANOVA sample size is unclear: The text first gives 59 participants after applying the “10 trials or less” rule, then removes one more participant from the main ANOVA because a cell had zero high-confidence responses. Since zero should already fall under “10 trials or less” unless the two sentences refer to different cell definitions, the final analysis N is not recoverable. State the exclusion sequence explicitly: how many participants entered the main ANOVA, which cells were checked at each step, and why the listwise-deletion case was not caught by the earlier criterion.
issues.quote:
Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design ( 10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 59 participants ( 5 participants were excluded). Included participants had on average $38.9 \%$ high confidence trial over all conditions (range: $8.4-64.4$, sd: 14.6). Excluded participants had on average $2.8 \%$ high confidence trials over all conditions (range $0.9-4.4 \%$, sd: 1.7 ).

The relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), and type of error (expectation induced illusory error - from pseudo-to-real or vice versa - or other error) as independent variables. Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA.

issues.subcategory: Real-to-pseudo errors are labelled as expectation-induced
issues.description: Real-to-pseudo errors are labelled as expectation-induced: Under the paper’s world-knowledge account, pseudo-to-real errors are expectation-congruent because the familiar real-letter form attracts the report. The reverse direction is not expectation-induced in the same sense. The analysis can still compare both directions, but the label should be neutral. Use “mirror-counterpart error” for the error-type factor, and reserve “expectation-induced” for the predicted excess of pseudo-to-real errors over real-to-pseudo errors.
issues.quote: The relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), and type of error (expectation induced illusory error - from pseudo-to-real or vice versa - or other error) as independent variables.

issues.subcategory: Balanced design shows imbalance is not necessary, not that it had no effect
issues.description: Balanced design shows imbalance is not necessary, not that it had no effect: Experiment 3 shows that the pseudo-to-real asymmetry can occur without the frequency imbalance used in Experiments 1 and 2. It does not by itself show that the imbalance made no contribution to the size of the earlier effects. Unless the paper compares effect sizes across the balanced and unbalanced designs, replace “highly unlikely explanation for the findings in Experiment 1-2” with the narrower conclusion that imbalance is not necessary for the effect. Also remove the circular phrase “as observed in Experiment 1-3”; Experiment 3 is the evidence being discussed.
issues.quote: The tendency to report more illusions in pseudo- than real-letter targets in Experiment 1-2 could have been due to the overrepresentation of real letters targets in the experiment. However, Experiment 3 shows that this is a highly unlikely explanation for the findings in Experiment 1-2: when letters and pseudo-letters are just as prevalent, participants still show the same pattern of results as observed in Experiment 1-3, with a stronger tendency to report, with high confidence, that they have seen a real letter, when in fact they were shown a pseudo-letter.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory comparison in Experiment 4 Results
issues.description: Contradictory comparison in Experiment 4 Results: The Experiment 4 Results sentence is internally contradictory: it says the increase in illusory errors was smaller for mirrored targets, but the reported values are $5\%$ for mirrored targets and $4\%$ for real-letter targets. This local wording error could confuse the interpretation of the non-supported three-way interaction, because the printed numbers indicate very similar effects, with the mirrored-target increase slightly larger rather than smaller.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored ( $5 \%$ difference) compared to when the target was a real letter ( $4 \%$ difference).

issues.subcategory: Incorrect experiment references for 500 ms delay
issues.description: Incorrect experiment references for 500 ms delay: The experiment references for the 500 ms summary appear incorrect: Experiment 1’s short delay was 0.75 s, while Experiment 4 also had a 500 ms condition. If the parenthetical is changed to Experiments 2 and 4, the “almost $20 \%$” summary may also need checking, since Experiment 4 reports $14 \%$ illusory responses at the short interval and Experiment 2’s short-delay rate depends on whether the value is averaged across target types or focused on pseudo-letter targets.
issues.quote: Illusory memories make up almost $20 \%$ of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2) and up to $30 \%$ of reports when memory is probed at 3 seconds (Experiment 1-4).

issues.subcategory: General Discussion overstates the temporal evidence
issues.description: General Discussion overstates the temporal evidence: The temporal increase in high-confidence pseudo-to-real errors supports a post-perceptual memory component, but the wording overreaches when it says participants “mainly start out with a correct percept” and that correctly encoded pseudo-letter percepts are “being converted” into real-letter memories. The experiments compare error rates across delays; they do not directly show the trial-level history of later illusory reports, nor do they show that perceptual or encoding illusions can account for only a small number of incorrect responses.
issues.quote: Experiments 1, 2 and 4 show that illusory memories make up a larger part of high confidence responses as time passes (from 0.5 s to 3 s ). This suggests that as the quality of the memory representation decreases through decay or interference, world knowledge plays an increasingly large role within STM. Also apparent from this increase in illusory memories over time, is that these incorrect responses are not just the result of errors in initial perception of the visual stimulus, or in encoding the stimulus incorrectly into memory. One can argue that expectations could very well shape perception, leading people to see (and thus report) a true letter when the visual input was a pseudo-letter. However, the increase in memory illusions over time suggests that, in our experiments, participants mainly start out with a correct percept, which they quite accurately report when probed early after the memory display has disappeared. Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter. So, perceptual illusions can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses, but memory illusions are also clearly present.

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of the baseline illusion rate
issues.description: Mischaracterization of the baseline illusion rate: The statement that perceptual illusions “can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses” is too strong. The delay-related increase supports a memory-driven component, but sizeable pseudo-to-real illusion rates are already present at the shortest probes, such as around 25–29% in Experiments 1–2. The data therefore do not determine how much of that early baseline reflects perceptual or encoding error versus very rapid memory distortion.
issues.quote: One can argue that expectations could very well shape perception, leading people to see (and thus report) a true letter when the visual input was a pseudo-letter. However, the increase in memory illusions over time suggests that, in our experiments, participants mainly start out with a correct percept, which they quite accurately report when probed early after the memory display has disappeared. Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter. So, perceptual illusions can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses, but memory illusions are also clearly present.

issues.subcategory: Predictive-processing section overlooks Experiment 3
issues.description: Predictive-processing section overlooks Experiment 3: The parenthetical generalisation about real-letter targets needs qualification: it fits Experiments 1, 2, and 4, but in Experiment 3 real-to-pseudo counterpart selections are reported at 13%, whereas other errors for real-letter targets are about 4%. Thus, in that balanced-stimulus experiment, real-to-pseudo errors do not appear to approximate ordinary other-item selections, even though the main pseudo-to-real asymmetry remains.
issues.quote: In predictive processing accounts of perception and cognition, the role that top-down information plays within cognition depends on the relative strength (or precision) of the bottom-up and top-down signals. In our experiments, top-down expectations for real letters can be expected to be relatively strong, as participants have been exposed to the standard alphabet frequently and from a young age. Pseudo-letters, on the other hand, will not have strong internal representations. Therefore, our finding that pseudo-letters are much more likely to give rise to real letter memory illusions, than the other way around, is expected: Memory traces for pseudo-letters are combined with strong internal priors for the real counterparts, making them more likely to result in illusory memories for the real letter. For real letter-targets the bottom-up memory information matches the internal predictions, and therefore the chance of formation of an illusory memory for the pseudo-letter counterpart of the real letter is small (although participants still sometimes select the pseudo-version of a real letter, but the incidence of these errors approximates the chance of selecting any other item in the display).

issues.subcategory: Weaker-trace argument in the origin section
issues.description: Weaker-trace argument in the origin section: The weaker-trace argument should account for the number of response alternatives in each error category. If selection were uniform across probe items, the single mirrored counterpart would not be expected to occur at a similar aggregate rate to pooled other errors; pooled other errors should generally be more frequent. The observed excess of illusory responses still argues against uniform guessing, but the stated null comparison is mathematically imprecise.
issues.quote:
However, our findings clearly show that pseudo-letter targets do not simply lead to weaker memory traces. If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target (or
more accurately, a participant easily forgetting a weakly established representation of a pseudo-letter target) should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability, as the representation of the target has been lost. This should result in similar rates of errors (selecting probe items that are not the target, or a mirrored version of the target) and illusions (selecting the mirrored version of the target). Our results show that this is not the case: Illusory memories are much more common than other errors when the target was a pseudo-letter. Moreover, the incidence of expectation induced illusory memories increases as the memory trace weakens, and this is not (or rather, much less) the case for other errors.

issues.subcategory: False equivalence in dismissing alternative hypothesis
issues.description: False equivalence in dismissing alternative hypothesis: The weaker-trace alternative is treated as if a weak trace must become a completely lost trace. A partially degraded trace could preserve letter identity or shape while losing orientation information, which would constrain responses mainly to the target and its mirrored counterpart rather than to all probe items. The present argument therefore does not by itself rule out a feature-specific degradation plus prior-based choice account.
issues.quote:
If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target (or
more accurately, a participant easily forgetting a weakly established representation of a pseudo-letter target) should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability, as the representation of the target has been lost. This should result in similar rates of errors (selecting probe items that are not the target, or a mirrored version of the target) and illusions (selecting the mirrored version of the target).

issues.subcategory: Mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory predictions
issues.description: Mischaracterization of Fuzzy Trace Theory predictions: The discussion of FTT may be too categorical. FTT includes mechanisms by which intact verbatim traces can support rejection of highly similar lures, but it can also predict false memories when verbatim or orientation-specific information is weak and decisions rely on gist. The passage should therefore distinguish the recollection-rejection prediction from possible gist-based predictions before concluding that FTT cannot account for the findings.
issues.quote: However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant. Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM.

issues.subcategory: Verbatim versus verbal in the FTT discussion
issues.description: Verbatim versus verbal in the FTT discussion: The FTT discussion moves too quickly from FTT’s verbatim/gist distinction to a verbal-rehearsal account. A verbatim trace in FTT is an exact representation of the experienced input, not necessarily a verbal label, so the prediction about articulatory suppression requires an additional assumption about verbal recoding that is not established here.
issues.quote: FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level ("mirrored") representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level. This would mean that verbal rehearsal is more effective to store a complete representation of real letters in working memory, but not for pseudo-letters. Removing verbal rehearsal as a strategy, for example through articulatory suppression, would therefore impact the storage of the verbal representation in working memory, leading to a decayed memory trace for real letters and pseudo-letters.

issues.subcategory: Overstatement about all STM stages in implications
issues.description: Overstatement about all STM stages in implications: The implications section overstates the stage-level conclusion. The preceding paragraph says that the experiments support illusory memories in WM-like and FM-like conditions but do not test IM, so the claim that all stages of STM are susceptible is stronger than the paper’s own taxonomy and evidence allow.
issues.quote:
The pervasiveness of illusory memories in STM
STM is often subdivided into Iconic Memory and Working memory. Iconic memory (IM), is a short-lived (<500 ms) high capacity memory storage, while working memory longer lasting, but with a smaller capacity of 2 to 4 items. It has been suggested that Fragile Memory constitutes an intermediate form of STM , which, like WM, lasts at least 4 seconds, but unlike WM has a capacity of $5-15$ items and is destroyed by visual interference. Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM. Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation, illusory memories are highly prevalent. Experiment $2-4$ show that in a FM set-up illusory memories are also abundant. Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM, which is sometimes thought not to be susceptible to illusions based on contextual information or internally generated biases .

The implications of STM illusory memories for vision research
The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research, as WM and IM tasks are often used to investigate the content of the visual percept for example in visual masking tasks or in change blindness tasks.

issues.subcategory: Overstatement of what the temporal delay proves
issues.description: Overstatement of what the temporal delay proves: The temporal increase in expectation-induced illusions supports the conclusion that memory processes contribute to the effect, but the wording here overstates what the delay manipulation proves. The increase shows that additional illusions emerge during retention; it does not establish that the short-delay illusions, or the specific traces that later produce errors, were initially stored correctly in STM.
issues.quote: In these 3 experiments, expectation-induced illusions became more prevalent as the delay between seeing the memory display and the memory probe increased. This shows that the illusions come into being while the memory trace is already (correctly) stored in STM.

{"overall": "Timing and the scope of post-perceptual memory change

In Experiments 1 and 2, the Short/Long manipulation varies the timing of the spatial cue, but the actual identity response and confidence judgement are taken later. In Experiment 1, the response follows a later irrelevant display; in Experiment 2, the response occurs 3.75 s after the memory-display offset. Readers might interpret the '500 ms' or '750 ms' conditions as early retrocue conditions rather than immediate report conditions.

This introduces the possibility that the delay effect reflects the selection and early consolidation of a cued item rather than prolonged maintenance of an uncued array. Leaving this ambiguity makes it complex to conclude that a correctly encoded item is actively converted into an illusory memory trace over the delay. Given the substantial pseudo-to-real rates already observed at the shortest delays—for example, 29% in Experiment 1 and 25% in Experiment 2—the delay-induced increase clearly supports memory-based exacerbation, but the temporal evidence does not yet cleanly isolate post-perceptual memory change from initial encoding dynamics.


Attrition and analysis of the high-confidence subset

The construct of a 'memory illusion' depends almost entirely on errors made with high confidence. The analyses condition on high-confidence trials, which results in excluding many participants due to insufficient high-confidence cell counts—most notably 17/40 participants in Experiment 1 and 92/290 in Experiment 2.

The included and excluded participants differ materially in their deployment of the top confidence category, meaning the analysed sample represents a sub-population specifically willing or able to give many high-confidence responses. If manipulations like delay, interference, or target type shift the baseline availability of the high-confidence response pool, proportional measures within that pool can rise even if the absolute frequency of an illusory report remains static. Providing full denominators, cell counts, confidence distributions, and examining trial-level hierarchical models that retain low-confidence participants will establish the robustness of this critical metric.


Disentangling false memory from orientation loss

The focal error measure involves participants selecting the mirrored counterpart of the target, whereas 'other errors' consist of selecting unrelated distractor letters. In Experiments 2–4, where both the target and its mirrored counterpart are present on the response screen, the task shifts toward an identity-plus-orientation discrimination.

Selecting the canonical letter could indicate that the identity of the letter was retained while its specific spatial orientation was lost, unbound, or normalised. Under an orientation-loss account, a participant could confidently report the canonical letter because the identity information is preserved, without actively requiring a vivid false visual memory of the orientation itself. The General Discussion notes that weak pseudo-letter traces should generate equal guessing across all probe items, but this argument does not directly address an identity-preserved, orientation-lost pathway.


Predictive processing versus recoding and maintenance

Experiments 3 and 4 successfully test for the local base-rate imbalances present in the initial studies. Balancing occurrence frequencies across the experiment, however, does not equate real and pseudo-letters on metrics of visual discriminability, verbal recodability, or maintenance strength.

A pseudo-letter memory trace could plausibly be encoded as a stable familiar letter name coupled with a fragile 'mirrored' tag.
